note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: Which of the following is a property of most metals?
items.explanation: Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity because their electrons are free to move.

options.why: Brittleness is typical of non-metals; metals bend rather than shatter.
Most metals have a characteristic shine called lustre.
Most metals are dense, though sodium and potassium are exceptions.

items.stem: Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
items.explanation: Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts because each carbon atom has a free electron.

options.why: Sulphur is an insulator like most non-metals.
Phosphorus does not conduct electricity.
Iodine is a non-conductor in its solid form.

items.stem: The property that lets a metal be beaten into thin sheets is called
items.explanation: Malleability is the ability to be hammered into sheets; ductility is the ability to be drawn into wires.

options.why: Ductility refers to being drawn into wires, not sheets.
Sonority is the property of making a ringing sound when struck.
Lustre is the shine of a freshly cut surface.

items.stem: Brass is an alloy of
items.explanation: Brass is made of copper and zinc.

options.why: Copper with tin gives bronze, not brass.
Iron with carbon gives steel.
Lead with tin gives solder.

items.stem: Which metal will displace copper from copper sulphate solution?
items.explanation: A metal above copper in the reactivity series can displace it; iron is above copper.

options.why: Silver lies below copper and cannot displace it.
Gold is the least reactive of these and displaces nothing.
Platinum lies below copper in the reactivity series.

items.stem: Heating a sulphide ore strongly in the presence of air is called
items.explanation: Roasting is used on sulphide ores; calcination heats carbonate ores in limited air.

options.why: Calcination is used for carbonate ores in limited air.
Smelting is reduction of an oxide with a reducing agent.
Refining purifies the metal after it has been extracted.

items.stem: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when
items.explanation: Conduction needs free ions, which exist only when the compound is molten or dissolved.

options.why: In a solid the ions are locked in the lattice and cannot move.
Powdering makes the pieces smaller but does not free the ions.
Warming alone does not free the ions until melting occurs.

items.stem: Aluminium oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. It is therefore
items.explanation: An oxide showing both acidic and basic behaviour is amphoteric.

options.why: A purely basic oxide would not react with sodium hydroxide.
A purely acidic oxide would not react with hydrochloric acid.
It reacts with both, so it is far from inert.

items.stem: In the electrolytic refining of copper, the impure metal is used as the
items.explanation: The impure metal is the anode and dissolves, while pure copper deposits on the cathode.

options.why: The cathode is a thin strip of pure copper on which metal deposits.
The electrolyte is acidified copper sulphate solution.
Anode mud is the insoluble impurity that collects below the anode.

items.stem: Sodium is stored under kerosene because it
items.explanation: Sodium reacts vigorously with both oxygen and moisture in air, and kerosene keeps both away.

options.text: reacts vigorously with air and moisture

options.why: Sodium does not dissolve in kerosene; the oil is merely a barrier.

options.text: is too soft to handle dry
options.why: Softness is a property but is not why it is kept under oil.
Sodium is a solid metal and does not evaporate at room temperature.

items.stem: Name the most ductile metal.
items.answer: Gold. It is the most ductile metal known, and one gram can be drawn into a wire about two kilometres long.

items.stem: Name a metal that is liquid at room temperature.
items.answer: Mercury. It is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature, which is why it was used in thermometers.

items.stem: What is the difference between a mineral and an ore?
items.answer: A mineral is any naturally occurring compound of a metal, while an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably. Every ore is a mineral, but not every mineral is rich enough to be an ore.

items.stem: Why does silver jewellery turn black over time?
items.answer: Silver reacts with the small amount of hydrogen sulphide in the air to form a thin black layer of silver sulphide on the surface. This is a form of corrosion called tarnishing.

items.stem: What is galvanisation?
items.answer: Galvanisation is the coating of iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc. The zinc keeps air and moisture away and, being more reactive, corrodes in preference to the iron even if the coating is scratched.

items.stem: Why are highly reactive metals extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?
items.answer: Their oxides are too stable for carbon to reduce, because the metals hold oxygen more strongly than carbon does. Electrolysis supplies electrical energy directly and can free the metal where a chemical reducing agent cannot.

items.stem: Why do sodium and chlorine combine in a one-to-one ratio?
items.answer: Sodium has one electron beyond a stable arrangement and loses it, while chlorine needs one electron to complete its outer shell. One electron transferred from each sodium atom satisfies one chlorine atom exactly, so the ratio is one to one.

items.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
items.answer: The oppositely charged ions are held in a rigid lattice by strong electrostatic forces acting in every direction. Breaking that lattice apart requires a large amount of energy, so the melting point is high.

items.stem: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals under four headings.
items.answer: Appearance: metals have a shine called lustre, while non-metals are generally dull, with iodine and graphite as exceptions. Physical state and hardness: metals are usually hard solids that can be bent, while non-metals are often soft solids, liquids or gases, and solid non-metals are brittle. Conductivity: metals conduct heat and electricity well because their electrons are free to move, while non-metals are poor conductors, with graphite the notable exception. Malleability and ductility: metals can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires, while non-metals shatter when struck. Metals are also sonorous, giving a ringing sound when struck, which is why bells are made of metal.

items.stem: What is an alloy, and why are alloys often preferred to pure metals? Give two examples.
items.answer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a small amount of a non-metal. Alloys are often preferred because alloying changes the properties in useful ways: it usually increases hardness and strength, lowers electrical conductivity, and can greatly improve resistance to corrosion. Steel, which is iron with a little carbon, is far harder and stronger than pure iron, which is soft. Stainless steel, iron with chromium and nickel, does not rust and is used for cutlery and surgical instruments. Brass, copper with zinc, is harder than copper and is used for fittings, while solder, lead with tin, has a low melting point which is exactly what is wanted for joining wires.

items.stem: Arrange zinc, iron, copper and magnesium in decreasing order of reactivity, and describe one experiment that would establish part of the order.
items.answer: The order is magnesium, then zinc, then iron, then copper. To establish part of it, take four test tubes of copper sulphate solution and place a clean strip of each metal in one of them. Magnesium, zinc and iron all give a red-brown deposit of copper and the blue colour fades, showing each is more reactive than copper, while the copper strip gives no change. To separate zinc from iron, place an iron nail in zinc sulphate solution and a zinc strip in iron sulphate solution. Only the second shows a change, which proves zinc is above iron. Repeating with magnesium against zinc sulphate completes the order. The principle throughout is that a metal displaces only a metal less reactive than itself.

items.stem: Outline the three main stages of extracting a metal from its ore.
items.answer: First, concentration of the ore, in which the unwanted earthy impurity called gangue is removed. The method depends on the ore and includes washing, magnetic separation and froth flotation. Second, conversion of the concentrated ore to the metal. A carbonate ore is calcined and a sulphide ore is roasted, both giving the oxide, and the oxide is then reduced. Moderately reactive metals are reduced by heating with carbon, while highly reactive metals must be obtained by electrolysis of the molten compound because carbon cannot reduce their oxides. Third, refining of the metal, most often by electrolytic refining, in which the impure metal is the anode and pure metal deposits on the cathode. The position of the metal in the reactivity series decides which route the middle stage must take.

items.stem: Describe an experiment showing that both air and water are needed for iron to rust.
items.answer: Take three test tubes, each with a clean iron nail. In the first, leave the nail in air with a drying agent such as anhydrous calcium chloride and close it with a stopper, so air is present but dry. In the second, cover the nail completely with water that has been boiled to drive out dissolved air, and seal the surface with a layer of oil, so water is present but air is not. In the third, leave the nail half in ordinary tap water and half exposed to the air. Leave all three for several days. The nail in dry air does not rust and the nail in air-free water does not rust, while the nail in the third tube rusts noticeably, most of all near the water line. Since rusting occurs only when both air and water are present, and is prevented by removing either, both are necessary.

items.stem: Explain why the method of extracting a metal depends on its position in the reactivity series.
items.answer: The position in the reactivity series measures how strongly a metal holds on to oxygen, or equivalently how readily it gives up electrons. Metals low in the series, such as gold and silver, are found free or need only gentle heating of their compounds, because their compounds are unstable. Metals in the middle, such as zinc, iron and lead, form oxides that carbon can reduce, so their ores are roasted or calcined to the oxide and then heated with coke; the reaction works because carbon has a greater affinity for oxygen than these metals do. Metals at the top, such as sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium, form oxides so stable that carbon cannot take the oxygen from them, and any attempt simply leaves the oxide unchanged. For these, electrolysis of the molten chloride or oxide is used, because an electric current can force the reduction that no chemical reducing agent will achieve. So the series does not merely list the metals, it predicts which extraction route is possible.

items.stem: Compare painting, oiling, galvanisation and alloying as ways of preventing rusting.
items.answer: All four work, but not in the same way, and this matters when the coating is damaged. Painting and oiling are pure barriers: they keep air and moisture off the surface, and they are cheap and easily applied, but a scratch exposes bare iron and rusting begins at once and can spread beneath the layer. Galvanisation is a barrier plus something more. Zinc keeps the air out, and because zinc is more reactive than iron it also corrodes in preference to the iron if the coating is scratched, so the iron stays protected even at a break. This is called sacrificial protection and is why galvanised sheeting lasts far longer than painted sheeting in the same conditions. Alloying does not coat the iron at all but changes it: adding chromium and nickel gives stainless steel, which forms its own thin invisible oxide layer that seals the surface permanently. Alloying is the most durable and the most expensive, galvanisation is the best value for structural use, and painting is chosen where cost and appearance matter more than longevity.

items.stem: Explain how an ionic bond forms between magnesium and chlorine, and deduce the formula.
items.answer: A magnesium atom has two electrons in its outermost shell beyond a stable arrangement, and it becomes stable by losing both, forming a magnesium ion with a charge of positive two. A chlorine atom is one electron short of a complete outer shell, so it becomes stable by gaining one electron, forming a chloride ion with a charge of negative one. One magnesium atom therefore has two electrons to give while each chlorine atom can accept only one, so two chlorine atoms are needed for every magnesium atom. The formula is MgCl2. The resulting ions carry opposite charges and attract one another strongly from every direction, so they pack into a regular three-dimensional lattice rather than forming separate molecules. This explains the properties of the compound: it is a hard, high-melting solid, it does not conduct in the solid state because the ions are fixed, and it conducts when molten or dissolved because the ions are then free to move.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Metals are good conductors of electricity. Reason (R): Metals have free electrons. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and free electrons carrying charge is exactly why metals conduct.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Mobile electrons carrying charge is precisely the mechanism of conduction.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Metals genuinely have delocalised free electrons.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Metals are among the best conductors known.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Solid sodium chloride conducts electricity. Reason (R): Sodium chloride is made of ions. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: the ions exist but are locked in the lattice and cannot move to carry charge.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Having ions is not enough; they must be free to move.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Sodium chloride genuinely is an ionic compound.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Solid sodium chloride is an insulator; molten or dissolved, it conducts.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A scratched galvanised sheet still resists rusting. Reason (R): Zinc is more reactive than iron. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and zinc's greater reactivity means it corrodes in preference to the iron, protecting it even at a break.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Sacrificial corrosion of the zinc is precisely why the scratch does not matter.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Zinc genuinely lies above iron in the reactivity series.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: This is the main advantage of galvanising over painting.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Copper can displace iron from iron sulphate solution. Reason (R): Copper is a metal and iron sulphate is a salt. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but irrelevant, and the assertion is false: copper lies below iron in the reactivity series and cannot displace it.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Being a metal is not enough; it must be the more reactive of the two.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Copper is a metal and iron sulphate is a salt, so the reason is true.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A copper strip in iron sulphate solution shows no change at all.

items.stem: State whether true or false: all non-metals are poor conductors of electricity.
items.explanation: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity well, so the statement is too strong.

options.why: Graphite conducts electricity and is used for electrodes.

items.stem: State whether true or false: metals can generally be drawn into wires.
items.explanation: Ductility is a characteristic property of metals.

options.why: Ductility lets metals be drawn into wires, which is why cables are metal.

items.stem: State whether true or false: calcination is used to convert a sulphide ore to its oxide.
items.explanation: Calcination treats carbonate ores in limited air; sulphide ores are roasted in plenty of air.

options.why: Sulphide ores are roasted; calcination is for carbonate ores.

items.stem: State whether true or false: all metallic oxides are basic.
items.explanation: Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric, reacting with both acids and bases.

options.why: Aluminium and zinc oxides are amphoteric, not purely basic.

items.stem: The ability of a metal to be drawn into thin wires is called ___________.
items.answer: ductility

items.stem: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature is ___________.
items.answer: mercury

items.stem: The unwanted earthy impurity present in an ore is called ___________.
items.answer: gangue

items.stem: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium and ___________.
items.answer: nickel

items.stem: Describe how metals react with oxygen, water and dilute acids, giving equations.
items.answer: With oxygen, metals form oxides, and the vigour depends on reactivity. Sodium and potassium react at room temperature and must be kept under oil. Magnesium burns with a dazzling flame, 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Iron and copper react only on strong heating, and gold does not react at all. The oxides formed are generally basic, though aluminium and zinc oxides are amphoteric. With water, potassium and sodium react violently at room temperature, releasing hydrogen that may catch fire: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. Magnesium reacts only with hot water, and iron reacts with steam: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Copper, silver and gold do not react with water at all. With dilute acids, any metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series displaces hydrogen: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2, and Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2. Metals below hydrogen, such as copper and silver, give no hydrogen with dilute acids. Nitric acid is an exception throughout, being an oxidising acid that gives nitrogen oxides rather than hydrogen.

items.stem: Describe the extraction of a moderately reactive metal from its sulphide ore, from ore to pure metal.
items.answer: Take zinc from zinc blende, ZnS, as the example. First the ore is concentrated to remove the gangue. Since the sulphide is wetted by oil and the earthy impurity by water, froth flotation is used: the powdered ore is stirred with water, pine oil and a little detergent, air is blown through, and the sulphide rises with the froth while the gangue sinks. Second the concentrated sulphide is roasted, that is heated strongly in plenty of air, converting it to the oxide and releasing sulphur dioxide: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. Roasting rather than calcination is used because the ore is a sulphide. Third the oxide is reduced by heating with coke, since zinc is in the middle of the reactivity series and carbon has a greater affinity for oxygen than zinc does: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Fourth the metal obtained is refined, usually by electrolytic refining, in which a block of the impure zinc is made the anode, a thin strip of pure zinc the cathode, and a zinc salt solution the electrolyte. Pure metal dissolves from the anode and deposits on the cathode, while the insoluble impurities collect below the anode as anode mud.

items.stem: Explain corrosion, why it matters economically, and how it is prevented.
items.answer: Corrosion is the gradual eating away of a metal surface by the action of air, moisture or chemicals around it. Different metals corrode differently: iron forms a reddish-brown flaky layer of hydrated iron oxide called rust, copper develops a green coating of basic copper carbonate, and silver forms a black layer of silver sulphide. Rust is the most damaging of these because it is porous and flaky, so it does not seal the surface and the corrosion continues inwards until the metal is weakened through. By contrast the oxide layer on aluminium is thin, hard and sticks firmly, so it protects the metal beneath, which is why aluminium survives outdoors while iron does not. Economically this matters a great deal, since bridges, railway lines, ships, vehicles and machinery are mostly iron and steel. A large fraction of annual steel production goes to replacing metal lost to rust, and failures caused by corrosion can be dangerous as well as costly. Prevention works either by keeping air and moisture out, using paint, grease, or a coating of another metal by galvanising, tinning or chromium plating, or by changing the metal itself through alloying, as in stainless steel. Galvanising is particularly effective because zinc both covers the iron and, being more reactive, corrodes sacrificially at any scratch, so the protection survives damage in a way that paint does not.

items.stem: Account for the physical properties of ionic compounds in terms of their structure.
items.answer: An ionic compound consists of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction. Crucially the attraction acts equally in all directions, so the ions pack into a regular repeating three-dimensional lattice rather than forming separate molecules. Every property follows from that structure. They are hard, because each ion is gripped by several neighbours of opposite charge. They have high melting and boiling points, because melting requires breaking a great many strong attractions throughout the lattice, which needs a large input of energy. They are brittle rather than malleable, because sliding one layer of the lattice over another brings ions of like charge face to face, and the resulting repulsion splits the crystal along a clean plane; this is why salt crystals shatter while metals bend. Many dissolve readily in water, because water molecules are polar and can surround and separate the ions, whereas they do not dissolve in non-polar solvents such as kerosene. They do not conduct electricity in the solid state, because although charged particles are present they are locked in position and cannot travel, but they conduct well when molten or dissolved, since the ions are then free to move towards the electrodes. The pattern worth noting is that the same two facts, strong attraction and a rigid ordered lattice, explain both what these compounds can do and what they cannot.

items.stem: An ore sample of mass 500 g yields 80 g of metal. Calculate the percentage of metal in the ore.
items.answer: The percentage is the mass of metal divided by the mass of ore, times 100. That is 80 divided by 500, times 100, which is 0.16 times 100, giving 16 per cent. The remaining 84 per cent is gangue and other impurity.

items.stem: A mine processes 2000 tonnes of ore containing 3 per cent copper, and 90 per cent of the copper is recovered. Find the mass of copper obtained.
items.answer: Copper present in the ore is 3 per cent of 2000 tonnes, that is 0.03 times 2000, which is 60 tonnes. Only 90 per cent of that is actually recovered, so the copper obtained is 0.90 times 60, which is 54 tonnes. The 6 tonnes not recovered is lost in the tailings and in the slag, which is why recovery efficiency matters as much as ore grade.

items.stem: An iron nail of mass 5.00 g is left in damp air and later weighs 5.36 g. Find the mass gained, its percentage, and explain where it came from.
items.answer: The mass gained is 5.36 g minus 5.00 g, which is 0.36 g. As a percentage of the original nail this is 0.36 divided by 5.00, times 100, which is 7.2 per cent. The gain is the mass of the oxygen and water that have chemically combined with the iron to form hydrated iron oxide. Those atoms came from the surrounding air and were not on the balance when the nail was first weighed, so the sample has gained mass while no matter has been created. This is also the clearest demonstration that rusting is a chemical change and not merely a surface discolouration: a physical change could not add mass.

items.stem: Match each alloy in Column I with its constituents in Column II. Column I: (a) brass, (b) bronze, (c) steel, (d) solder. Column II: (i) iron and carbon, (ii) lead and tin, (iii) copper and zinc, (iv) copper and tin.
items.answer: (a) brass - (iii) copper and zinc. (b) bronze - (iv) copper and tin. (c) steel - (i) iron and carbon. (d) solder - (ii) lead and tin.

items.stem: Match each protective method in Column I with the coating metal or agent in Column II. Column I: (a) galvanisation, (b) tinning, (c) painting, (d) alloying for stainless steel. Column II: (i) tin, (ii) chromium and nickel, (iii) zinc, (iv) a barrier layer of pigment.
items.answer: (a) galvanisation - (iii) zinc, which also protects sacrificially. (b) tinning - (i) tin, used inside food cans. (c) painting - (iv) a barrier layer of pigment. (d) stainless steel - (ii) chromium and nickel alloyed into the iron.

items.stem: Draw and label the apparatus for the electrolytic refining of copper, marking where pure metal forms.
items.answer: Draw a tank containing acidified copper sulphate solution as the electrolyte. Suspend a thick block of impure copper on the left, connected to the positive terminal of a battery, and label it anode, impure copper. Suspend a thin strip of pure copper on the right, connected to the negative terminal, and label it cathode, pure copper. Label the solution as the electrolyte, acidified copper sulphate. Show a layer of sediment beneath the anode and label it anode mud, containing the insoluble impurities. Draw arrows showing copper ions travelling through the solution from anode to cathode, and mark the direction of the current in the external circuit. Annotate that the anode dissolves and loses mass while pure copper deposits on the cathode, which gains mass, and that soluble impurities remain in the solution while insoluble ones fall as anode mud. Note beside the diagram that the purity achieved is above 99.9 per cent, which is why this method is used for the copper in electrical wiring.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of the reactivity series and annotate it with what each region implies for extraction.
items.answer: Draw a vertical arrow or ladder with the most reactive metals at the top and the least at the bottom, and mark the metals in order: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, then hydrogen as a reference line, then copper, silver, gold and platinum. Draw a clear horizontal line at hydrogen and label it: metals above this line displace hydrogen from dilute acids, those below do not. Now bracket the ladder into three regions and annotate each. The top region, from potassium to aluminium, is labelled extracted by electrolysis of the molten compound, because their oxides are too stable for carbon to reduce. The middle region, from zinc to lead, is labelled ore roasted or calcined to the oxide, then reduced by heating with carbon. The bottom region, from copper to platinum, is labelled found free in nature or obtained by gentle heating, because their compounds are unstable. Add a further annotation that a metal displaces from solution only a metal below it, and mark two example arrows: iron displacing copper, and copper failing to displace iron. Finally note that reactivity here means the readiness to give up electrons, which is why the same single order predicts behaviour with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions alike.

items.stem: Design and describe an experiment that establishes the relative reactivity of zinc, iron and copper.
items.answer: Prepare fresh solutions of zinc sulphate, iron sulphate and copper sulphate, and clean strips of zinc, iron and copper with sandpaper so that no oxide layer remains. Set up nine test tubes so that every metal is tested against every solution, including the metal in its own salt as a control. Leave them undisturbed for about twenty minutes and record every observation. The results are as follows. Zinc in iron sulphate gives a dark deposit on the strip and the green colour fades, so zinc displaces iron. Zinc in copper sulphate gives a red-brown deposit and the blue colour fades, so zinc displaces copper. Iron in copper sulphate gives a red-brown deposit and the blue fades to pale green, so iron displaces copper. Iron in zinc sulphate shows no change, so iron does not displace zinc. Copper in zinc sulphate and copper in iron sulphate both show no change, so copper displaces neither. Each metal in its own salt shows no change, confirming that the observed deposits are genuine displacements and not a reaction with the water or the tube. Now reason from the results. A metal displaces another from solution only if it is the more reactive of the two. Zinc displaced both iron and copper, so zinc is above both. Iron displaced copper but was itself displaced by zinc, so iron sits between them. Copper displaced nothing and was displaced by both, so copper is the least reactive. The established order is therefore zinc, then iron, then copper. The controls matter to the proof: without them, a deposit could be attributed to something other than displacement, and the negative results are as important as the positive ones because they rule out the reverse orderings.
